nameStory: The "wheatear" name comes from the Old English "white" and "ears," referring to the bird's distinctive white rump patch that flashes prominently when it flies. This conspicuous white marking was so eye-catching to early observers that they named the entire bird after what looked like white "ears" on its backside. The "northern" part simply distinguishes it from other wheatear species found further south.
description: The Northern Wheatear is a small, robin-sized songbird that's quite rare in New England but occasionally shows up during migration. These compact birds are about 6 inches long with a distinctive upright posture when perched on rocks or posts. They have a grayish-blue back, peachy-buff underparts, a black eye stripe, and most notably, a bright white rump patch that flashes like a beacon when they fly. Think of them as having the build of a small thrush but the behavior of a flycatcher.

idTips.label: White rump flash
idTips.description: The most obvious field mark is a brilliant white rump and base of tail that creates a striking flash pattern in flight, visible from quite a distance and unmistakable once seen

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Sits very upright on prominent perches like fence posts, rocks, or bush tops, often flicking its tail and appearing alert and nervous

idTips.label: Black eye stripe
idTips.description: Shows a distinctive black stripe through the eye like a mask, contrasting with lighter gray-blue upperparts

idTips.label: Ground foraging
idTips.description: Frequently drops to the ground to catch insects, then returns to its perch, moving with quick, jerky hops on the ground

idTips.label: Tail pattern
idTips.description: Black tail with white base forms an inverted 'T' pattern when spread, especially visible during short flights between perches

habitat: In New England, Northern Wheatears are most likely found in open, rocky areas during migration, especially coastal headlands, airport fields, golf courses, and similar short-grass habitats. They prefer areas with scattered rocks, posts, or low shrubs that provide perching spots overlooking open ground where they can spot insects. Look for them in places that remind you of moorland or tundra - wide open spaces with minimal tree cover.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring migrants may appear in late April through May, usually single birds stopping briefly in suitable open habitat during their journey north.
seasonality.summer: Extremely unlikely to be seen in summer as they breed in arctic regions far north of New England.
seasonality.fall: Most New England sightings occur during fall migration from late August through October, when birds occasionally appear along the coast during their epic journey to Africa.
seasonality.winter: Never present in winter as all Northern Wheatears spend this season in Africa, making one of the longest migrations of any small songbird.

funFact: Northern Wheatears make one of the most incredible migrations in the bird world - some individuals breeding in Alaska actually fly all the way across Asia and Europe to spend winter in Africa, a journey of over 15,000 miles that takes them through three continents!
confusionNotes: The white rump flash is so distinctive that Northern Wheatears are rarely confused with other birds once you see them fly. The closest confusion might be with a Northern Mockingbird, but mockingbirds are much larger, have white wing patches (not rump), and lack the black eye stripe. Remember: "Wheatear = white rear!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, Northern Wheatears have nothing to do with wheat or ears of grain - this is purely about the white rump patch that early English speakers thought looked like white "ears." These birds are actually members of the Old World flycatcher family, more closely related to European robins than to American birds, which explains their somewhat unusual appearance in our landscape.
compareHints: Northern Wheatears are the only member of their genus regularly seen in North America, making them fairly unique. Within the broader flycatcher family, they're much more terrestrial than most flycatchers, spending more time on the ground and lacking the typical flycatcher habit of returning to the exact same perch. Their upright posture and ground-foraging behavior actually make them more similar to American Robins in behavior, though they're much smaller and have that unmistakable white rump flash.
